title: Teaching hospital pre-assessment clinic: perioperative glucose protocol, a late reply refused and a trial replaced by a feasibility study
notes: Expert path. The need names a randomised trial, so routing is 'rct' at create. The problem reply returns constraints null: the investigator's typed constraints stay unchanged with issue rejected-change (G11; S5 named because no listed entry defines the code). A fixture search returns seven records. The first scan appraisal is a late reply: the request goes out, the investigator edits the constraints while it is pending (orthopaedic lists cannot schedule patients first), and the reply produced against the earlier study revision must be refused by the studyRevision guard: nothing applied, stage still incomplete, the refusal shown and logged (G6; A3.1 item 1). The stats stage then shows that about 340 patients would be needed, nearly five years at this hospital. A second design reply recommends a single-site feasibility study with progression criteria; it flags the completed protocol and stats stages for review (G8), the investigator withdraws the first decision and accepts the second, so the family becomes 'feasibility' only on acceptance (S11), and re-running protocol and stats clears the review flags. inputs.need:
I am a consultant anaesthetist at Castlemere University Hospital, a 500-bed teaching hospital, and I lead our pre-assessment clinic. Patients with insulin-treated diabetes who come in for elective surgery are managed according to whatever the ward and theatre teams remember: some have their long-acting insulin reduced the night before, some omit it altogether, and some are started on a variable-rate insulin infusion that then runs for days. Our pre-assessment audit last year found that 31 of 112 insulin-treated patients had a capillary glucose above 12 mmol/L on the day of surgery, and 9 had a value below 4 mmol/L in the 24 hours after surgery.

We have written a perioperative glucose management protocol with four parts: a personal dose-adjustment table handed out at pre-assessment, a diabetes specialist nurse phone call two days before surgery, first-on-the-list scheduling where possible, and a subcutaneous correction scale instead of routine infusions for shorter operations. I would like to run a randomised trial comparing the protocol with usual care, with glucose out of range on the day of surgery as the main outcome, but I am not sure how many patients we would need or whether our lists can cope with first-on-the-list scheduling. We see about 150 insulin-treated patients a year for elective general, orthopaedic and urological surgery.

The diabetes team supports the idea, but their specialist nurse has only a few hours a week. We have no continuous glucose monitors for surgical patients, so everything depends on finger-prick measurements. I would also like to hear from patients, because several have told us that conflicting instructions from different staff are the worst part of the experience, and I want the study to measure that too.
inputs.constraints: The diabetes specialist nurse can give 4 hours a week. Capillary glucose meters only; no continuous glucose monitors. First-on-the-list scheduling needs the agreement of each surgical specialty. No funding beyond a departmental grant of 12,000.

response.title: Perioperative glucose management protocol for insulin-treated patients having elective surgery
response.subtitle: Evaluation design to be settled against recruitment and theatre scheduling
response.statement: Insulin-treated patients having elective surgery at a teaching hospital receive inconsistent perioperative glucose management: variable insulin advice, infusions that run for days, and conflicting instructions. A local review found out-of-range capillary glucose on the day of surgery in 31 of 112 patients and postoperative values below 4 mmol/L in 9. A four-part protocol has been written; its effect on day-of-surgery glucose and its deliverability across general, orthopaedic and urological surgery are unknown.
response.whoAffected: About 150 insulin-treated adults a year having elective surgery, the pre-assessment and diabetes teams, theatre and ward staff.
response.whatHurts: Hyperglycaemia is associated with infection and hypoglycaemia while fasting is dangerous; conflicting instructions lead patients to change insulin on their own.
response.currentPractice: No written protocol; insulin advice varies by who sees the patient; infusions are started by default.
response.whyNow: A protocol is ready, a small departmental grant has been awarded, and the diabetes team is willing.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients receive one clear plan for their insulin, stay in a safe glucose range, and are not left fasting and uncertain.
response.summary: Problem framed around a four-part perioperative glucose protocol whose effect and deliverability are unknown.

records.title: A pre-assessment insulin dose-adjustment plan and day-of-surgery glucose: a before-after study
records.authors: Ferreira-Mensah D, Holloway-Iwu K, Lindgren-Obasi T
records.abstract: We introduced a written insulin dose-adjustment plan, handed to patients at pre-assessment, for adults with insulin-treated diabetes having elective surgery, and compared 214 patients after the change with 198 before. Out-of-range glucose on the day of surgery, defined as a capillary value above 12 or below 4 mmol/L, fell from 34 percent to 21 percent. Use of variable-rate insulin infusions fell from 46 to 18 percent of patients. Hypoglycaemia in the 24 hours after surgery was similar (6 against 5 percent). The comparison was uncontrolled, and staff awareness of the evaluation may have changed practice beyond the plan itself.

records.title: Specialist nurse telephone contact before elective surgery for people with insulin-treated diabetes: a pilot randomised trial
records.abstract: We randomised 60 adults with insulin-treated diabetes to a diabetes specialist nurse phone call two days before elective surgery or to usual care. Recruitment was 48 percent of eligible patients, meeting the progression criterion of 40 percent, and 94 percent of intervention patients received the call. Out-of-range glucose on the day of surgery occurred in 30 percent of intervention and 43 percent of usual-care patients, an imprecise difference. Outcome data were complete for 79 percent, below the 90 percent criterion, mainly because capillary values were not documented on the ward. The authors did not proceed to a definitive trial.

records.title: First-on-the-list scheduling for patients with diabetes: feasibility across surgical specialties
records.abstract: We measured how often adults with diabetes could be scheduled first on the morning operating list in three hospitals over one year. First-on-the-list scheduling was achieved for 71 percent of general surgery patients, 38 percent of orthopaedic patients and 64 percent of urology patients. Orthopaedic lists were often reordered for implant availability and trauma. When achieved, fasting time fell by a mean of 3.1 hours. Surgeons and theatre managers supported the principle but reported that it competed with other scheduling priorities such as children and patients with latex allergy.

records.title: Subcutaneous correction scales versus variable-rate insulin infusion for short elective operations: a cohort study
records.authors: Brennan-Achterberg L, Moyo-Hartmann J, Silva-Okafor N
records.abstract: In 1,020 elective operations lasting under three hours in adults with insulin-treated diabetes, we compared patients managed with a subcutaneous insulin correction scale with those started on a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion. Hypoglycaemia below 4 mmol/L within 24 hours occurred in 4 percent with the correction scale and 9 percent with the infusion. Hyperglycaemia above 12 mmol/L was similar in both groups. Patients started on an infusion were older and had longer operations, so confounding by indication is likely. Infusions continued for more than 24 hours in 31 percent of infusion patients.

records.title: Perioperative hyperglycaemia and surgical site infection in patients with diabetes: a systematic review
records.authors: Tanaka-Ruiz E, Obi-Lindahl C, Graves-Mbatha P, Holm-Adebayo R
records.abstract: We searched four databases to 2020 for studies of perioperative glucose and surgical site infection in adults with diabetes. Nineteen studies met the criteria, most of them observational. Glucose above 10 to 12 mmol/L around the time of surgery was associated with higher odds of surgical site infection (pooled odds ratio 1.8, 95 percent CI 1.4 to 2.3), with moderate heterogeneity. Thresholds and timing of glucose measurement varied between studies. Two small trials of tighter perioperative control did not show a clear reduction in infection, and one reported more hypoglycaemia.

records.title: Patients' experience of conflicting diabetes instructions before surgery: a qualitative study
records.abstract: We spoke with 22 adults with insulin-treated diabetes after elective surgery about the instructions they had received. Most described receiving different advice about their insulin from the pre-assessment clinic, the surgical team and the ward. Several reduced or stopped insulin on their own because they feared low glucose while fasting. Participants valued a single written plan that all staff followed and a named person to call. Patients who had surgery late in the day described the longest periods of uncertainty. Participants were recruited from one hospital.

records.title: Capillary glucose meter accuracy in the perioperative period
records.abstract: We compared 410 paired capillary meter and laboratory glucose values in surgical patients before, during and after operations. Above 5.5 mmol/L, 95 percent of meter values were within 15 percent of the laboratory value. Below 4 mmol/L, agreement was poorer and meters tended to read high, which could delay recognition of hypoglycaemia. Low haematocrit after blood loss increased the meter bias. The authors recommend laboratory confirmation of low meter values and caution when meters are the only measure of hypoglycaemia in perioperative studies.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level against the revised constraints. A pre-assessment dose plan was followed by fewer out-of-range values (34 to 21 percent) and correction scales by less hypoglycaemia than infusions, both in observational studies. A pilot trial of a nurse call recruited adequately but failed on outcome completeness because ward values were not documented. First-on-the-list scheduling is unreliable in orthopaedics, which matches the new constraint. Patients want one plan and one contact. Low meter readings need laboratory confirmation.
response.gradeRationale: Observational before-after and cohort evidence, one small pilot trial and qualitative data; consistent direction, serious risk of bias and imprecision.

response.reading: The protocol's four parts act at different points: the dose plan and the nurse call before admission, scheduling on the day, and the correction scale after surgery. Evidence supports each part weakly and separately. The practical risks for any evaluation are recruitment, documentation of ward capillary values, and scheduling that works in general surgery and urology but not orthopaedics.

At about 150 eligible patients a year and the 48 percent recruitment seen in a comparable pilot, the hospital would randomise about 72 a year, so recruitment would take nearly five years. A definitive single-site trial is not feasible; a feasibility study or a multicentre trial would be needed.

response.designSummary: Single-arm feasibility study; estimation of recruitment, delivery and completeness rates against progression criteria.
response.sampleSize: About 112 eligible patients are expected in nine months. With 112 eligible patients, a recruitment rate near 50 percent is estimated within about 9 percentage points (95 percent confidence). With about 56 recruited patients, delivery and completeness rates near 85 to 90 percent are estimated within about 8 to 9 points. This is enough to judge the progression criteria, not to estimate an effect.
response.primaryAnalysis: Recruitment rate with a 95 percent confidence interval, compared with the 50 percent criterion; a traffic-light rule (proceed, amend, stop) fixed in advance.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Delivery and completeness rates against their criteria; proportion with glucose out of range and its interval to inform a trial sample size; questionnaire scores.
response.missingData: Missing glucose values are the completeness outcome itself and are reported, not imputed.
response.multiplicity: No hypothesis tests; three criteria judged by pre-specified rules.
overfittingGuards: No effect estimate reported as efficacy
response.summary: Precision adequate to judge three progression criteria.

response.risks: The protocol changes insulin management, with a small risk of hypoglycaemia while fasting; low values are confirmed in the laboratory and treated by the ward's existing policy.
response.consent: Written informed consent at pre-assessment for the protocol's research data collection and the questionnaire; patients who decline receive usual care and are counted anonymously in the recruitment log.
response.data: Study charts are coded; the key stays in the pre-assessment clinic; only coded data enter the analysis.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients with limited English receive the dose table in their language and interpreter-supported calls; patients in orthopaedics, who cannot be scheduled first, are reported separately so the protocol is shown to work without scheduling.
response.effectiveness: Decides whether a multicentre trial is worth running.
response.efficiency: Uses the nurse's existing hours and the departmental grant.
response.costs: Study charts, translation of the dose table, and research nurse time within the 12,000 grant.
response.grants: Departmental grant DRG-2026-09; a multicentre trial would need external funding.
response.partnerships: Diabetes team, theatre managers for general surgery and urology, two patient partners with insulin-treated diabetes.
response.rebPath: Hospital research ethics committee review under ICH-GCP and the Declaration of Helsinki before any recruitment; the committee has not yet reviewed any version.
response.limitations: Single site; no comparison group; staff attention may inflate delivery.

response.title: A perioperative glucose management protocol for insulin-treated patients having elective surgery: a single-site feasibility study
response.abstract: Objective: to assess recruitment, protocol delivery and outcome completeness for a four-part perioperative glucose protocol against pre-specified progression criteria. Design: single-arm feasibility study over nine months at one teaching hospital. Participants: adults with insulin-treated diabetes having elective general, orthopaedic or urological surgery. Results will be reported after recruitment ends.
response.introduction: Perioperative glucose management for insulin-treated patients varies between staff, and patients report conflicting instructions. A definitive randomised trial at one hospital would need about 340 participants and nearly five years, and a comparable pilot trial failed on outcome completeness.
response.methods: Consecutive eligible patients are invited at pre-assessment; the dose table, the nurse call and scheduling are logged. Capillary glucose is recorded on a study chart at fixed times for 24 hours, with laboratory confirmation of values below 4 mmol/L. Progression criteria are at least 50 percent recruitment, 80 percent protocol delivery and 90 percent outcome completeness, judged by a traffic-light rule fixed in advance.
response.results: Recruitment has not started; ethics review is pending.
response.discussion: The discussion will apply the traffic-light rules and describe what a multicentre trial would need. Orthopaedic patients, who cannot be scheduled first, will be reported separately.
response.limitations: No comparison group; one site; staff attention during the study may inflate delivery rates.
response.conclusion: To be written after recruitment ends. It will report feasibility, not effectiveness.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for pilot and feasibility trials, items applicable to a single-arm design

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am a consultant anaesthetist at Castlemere University Hospital, a 500-bed teaching hospital, and I lead our pre-assessment clinic. Patients with insulin-treated diabetes who come in for elective surgery are managed according to whatever the ward and theatre teams remember: some have their long-acting insulin reduced the night before, some omit it altogether, and some are started on a variable-rate insulin infusion that then runs for days. Our pre-assessment audit last year found that 31 of 112 insulin-treated patients had a capillary glucose above 12 mmol/L on the day of surgery, and 9 had a value below 4 mmol/L in the 24 hours after surgery.

We have written a perioperative glucose management protocol with four parts: a personal dose-adjustment table handed out at pre-assessment, a diabetes specialist nurse phone call two days before surgery, first-on-the-list scheduling where possible, and a subcutaneous correction scale instead of routine infusions for shorter operations. I would like to run a randomised trial comparing the protocol with usual care, with glucose out of range on the day of surgery as the main outcome, but I am not sure how many patients we would need or whether our lists can cope with first-on-the-list scheduling. We see about 150 insulin-treated patients a year for elective general, orthopaedic and urological surgery.

The diabetes team supports the idea, but their specialist nurse has only a few hours a week. We have no continuous glucose monitors for surgical patients, so everything depends on finger-prick measurements. I would also like to hear from patients, because several have told us that conflicting instructions from different staff are the worst part of the experience, and I want the study to measure that too.
